title: Evil as corruption (7.12)
hookLine: whatever is, is good; evil is the spoiling of a good
tomorrow: why would a well-known old teacher risk saying it out loud?

lines: A PEACH WITH A SOFT SPOT.
cards: A peach on the counter with a soft brown spot. The spot is real, and it's spreading. But ask what it's eating, and the answer is peach.
Good peach. If there were no peach left, there'd be no spot either. Augustine had been asking the big version of that for a long time: if God is good and made everything, where does evil come from?
In book seven he lands on an answer that still starts arguments. The rot isn't a thing. It's a good thing, being spoiled.

teach.b: Here's his case. Things that can be spoiled are good. If they were supremely good, nothing could spoil them.
If they had no good in them at all, there'd be nothing to spoil. Corruption only harms by taking good away, and take away all the good, and the thing itself is gone. So: whatever is, is good.
Evil isn't a substance. It's the spoiling of a good. He ties it to Genesis, in the Douay-Rheims: "And God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good."
Now the other side, and some readers press it hard.
Doesn't that make evil sound small, a hole, a missing piece? Say that to someone grieving. And the Church also speaks of a real enemy: the Catechism names the devil, a fallen angel.
Augustine's side answers in two moves.

teach.h: A HOLE CAN SINK A SHIP.
teach.b: A hole can sink a ship; blindness is only missing sight, and nobody calls it small.

teach.h: EVEN THE FALLEN WERE MADE GOOD.
teach.b: And the Catechism itself says the devil and the other demons were created naturally good by God, and became evil by their own doing.
So even there, the rot is eating something good. Both sides take evil seriously. They differ on what it's made of, and on whether that answer comforts or stings.

how: The Catechism teaches that God created everything good and that evil is not something God made; Catholic theology, following Augustine, speaks of evil as a privation, the lack of a good that should be there.

o: a second force as strong as goodness
a dark power God made to test people
a good thing spoiled, not a thing in itself

games.q: all that is, is good — tap the pairs.

s: the harm is real. his claim is narrower: evil isn't a substance, it's a good thing spoiled.
the Catechism says the devil was created naturally good
and became evil by his own doing.
if all the good were taken out of a thing, its evil would remain
Augustine says the thing itself would be gone. no good left, nothing left to spoil.

games.q: you like Augustine's answer. your friend doesn't. before you reply, which is the fairest way to put her side?
o: "calling evil a lack can sound like it shrinks real suffering."
"she just hasn't read enough Augustine to get it yet."
"she thinks God made evil on purpose to hurt people."
games.why: that's the real objection some readers raise. Augustine's side answers it: a hole can sink a ship, and blindness is only a lack, yet nobody calls it small.

practice: Find something spoiled within reach: a chipped mug, a scuffed shoe, a bruised piece of fruit. Look past the damage to the good thing it's spoiling, and name that good to yourself. If you pray, you can give thanks for it.

wordCard.voice: Evil as corruption. Augustine's answer in book seven: evil is not a thing God made, but the spoiling of a good.

orig.note: Latin, Confessions 7.12: whatever things are, are good.

carryVoice: All that is, is good, and the rot is real because the good was there first. Day done.
